## Why this guide exists

Terrain-based watershed delineation is one of the first things people run in a GIS
and one of the last things they read the documentation for. The workflow is short
enough to copy from a blog post: hand a digital elevation model to a flow routing
tool, pick a threshold, get streams and basins. It runs in seconds, it returns a
map that looks authoritative, and almost nothing about the result announces which
of your choices produced it.

This guide walks the whole workflow in GRASS using
[`r.watershed`](https://grass.osgeo.org/grass-stable/manuals/r.watershed.html),
and spends most of its length on the parts that change the answer:

- the computational region, which is a model parameter here and not a display setting,
- the difference between a NULL gap and a depression, which must be handled in
  opposite ways,
- `threshold`, which is counted in cells and therefore depends on resolution,
- the flow routing method, multiple flow direction by default and single flow with a flag,
- the sign of the accumulation raster, which is a warning and not a rendering nuisance.

Everything below runs on your own machine with a package-manager install of GRASS
and the free Flagstaff sample dataset. Nothing here needs an account, a cloud
service, or a network connection past the one download.

::: {.callout-note}
## Who this is for

You know what a watershed is and you have run a flow accumulation tool before,
possibly in another package. You have not necessarily used GRASS. If you have
never opened GRASS at all, the
[first-time users page](https://grass.osgeo.org/learn/newcomers/) is a better
starting point, then come back.
:::

## Data and tools

### Dataset

| Item | Value |
|------|-------|
| Name | Flagstaff, Arizona sample dataset, `flagstaff_az_usa_epsg6341` |
| Map used | `elevation`, a 30 m DEM covering the watersheds around Flagstaff, Coconino County, Arizona, USA |
| CRS | NAD83(2011) / UTM zone 12N (EPSG:6341), metres |
| Elevation source | USGS, patched from the `n35_w112_1arc` and `n34_w112_1arc` tiles, reprojected to EPSG:6341 at 30 m and clipped to the region |
| Compiled by | Michael Barton and Eunice Villasenor, Arizona State University |
| Funding | NSF POSE Phase II, "Growing GRASS OSE for Worldwide Access to Multidisciplinary Geospatial Analytics", grant FAIN-2303651, lead PI Helena Mitasova, NC State University |
| Terms | Published by the GRASS project as a sample dataset for research, development and education, assembled from public agency sources (USGS, NRCS, Data.gov, Coconino County, City of Flagstaff GIS, Arizona state GIS). Credit the compilers and the originating agencies when you publish from it. |
| Download | <https://grass.osgeo.org/sampledata/flagstaff_az_usa_epsg6341.zip> (about 89 MB) |
| Accessed | 2026-09-04 |

Two properties of this dataset matter for what follows, and both are unusual in a
teaching DEM.

The region is not a rectangle drawn for convenience. Its boundaries follow the
watersheds surrounding the city, so the area very nearly contains its own
drainage rather than slicing through the middle of somebody else's. That makes
the edge effects discussed later small and legible instead of overwhelming.

The dataset also ships a `watersheds` vector taken from the City of Flagstaff's
own GIS. That gives us a published delineation to compare against, which turns
the usual hand-waving about "your basins will not match the official ones" into
something we can actually put on a map.

Every non-obvious module used below, with the authorship recorded in the module's
own manual page. Citing the people who wrote the algorithm is cheap and it is the
norm in this community.

### Versions

The exact software this page was rendered against is printed by the code below, so
the numbers in the output are attributable to a specific build rather than to
"GRASS" in the abstract.

```{python}
# | label: versions
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

# Ask GRASS where its Python package lives and put it on the path.
sys.path.append(
    subprocess.check_output(["grass", "--config", "python_path"], text=True).strip()
)

import grass.script as gs  # noqa: E402
import grass.jupyter as gj  # noqa: E402

print(subprocess.check_output(["grass", "--version"], text=True).splitlines()[0])
print("Python", sys.version.split()[0])
```

The analysis below is written against `grass.tools`, the object API added in
GRASS 8.4. Tools are methods, so `r.watershed` is `tools.r_watershed(...)`,
keyword arguments are the module's own options, and `format="json"` gives back
something you can subscript instead of a string you have to parse. The older
`grass.script.run_command` still works and appears here only where `grass.tools`
has no equivalent, such as switching mapsets.

## Get the sample dataset

The cell below downloads and unpacks the Flagstaff dataset if it is not already
on disk. It is idempotent: if you already have `flagstaff_az_usa_epsg6341` under
`~/grassdata`, nothing is downloaded.

```{python}
# | label: sample-data
import zipfile
import urllib.request

GRASSDATA = Path.home() / "grassdata"
PROJECT = GRASSDATA / "flagstaff_az_usa_epsg6341"
URL = "https://grass.osgeo.org/sampledata/flagstaff_az_usa_epsg6341.zip"

if not PROJECT.exists():
    GRASSDATA.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    archive = GRASSDATA / "flagstaff_az_usa_epsg6341.zip"
    print(f"Downloading {URL} (about 89 MB)")
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(URL, archive)
    with zipfile.ZipFile(archive) as zf:
        zf.extractall(GRASSDATA)
    archive.unlink()

print("Project:", Path("~") / PROJECT.relative_to(Path.home()))
print("PERMANENT mapset present:", (PROJECT / "PERMANENT").is_dir())
```

Start a session in the project and switch to a dedicated mapset. Writing results
into their own mapset keeps `PERMANENT` clean, which matters more than it sounds:
`PERMANENT` holds the project definition and the reference data, and a tutorial
that scribbles on it is a tutorial you cannot rerun from a known state.

```{python}
# | label: session
session = gj.init(PROJECT / "PERMANENT")

from grass.tools import Tools  # noqa: E402

# Switching mapsets is still a grass.script call: g.mapset changes the session
# the Tools object is bound to, so it has to happen before Tools() is built.
existing = gs.read_command("g.mapsets", flags="l").split()
gs.run_command(
    "g.mapset", mapset="watershed", flags="" if "watershed" in existing else "c"
)

tools = Tools()
print(gs.read_command("g.mapset", flags="p").strip())
```

## The computational region is a model parameter

In GRASS, raster operations run over the computational region: an extent plus a
cell size, held separately from any particular map. Set it once and every raster
module reads and writes at that resolution.

That is the piece people coming from other tools miss. Here the region is not a
zoom level or a display preference. It is the grid the model runs on, and
`r.watershed` counts cells, so the region resolution enters the science directly.

```{python}
# | label: region
tools.g_region(raster="elevation@PERMANENT")
region = tools.g_region(flags="p", format="json")
n_cells = region["rows"] * region["cols"]

print(f"resolution: {region['nsres']:.0f} m")
print(f"grid:       {region['rows']} rows x {region['cols']} cols")
print(f"cells:      {n_cells:,}")
print(f"extent:     {(region['east'] - region['west']) / 1000:.1f} km east-west, "
      f"{(region['north'] - region['south']) / 1000:.1f} km north-south")

cell_area_m2 = region["nsres"] * region["ewres"]
print(f"cell area:  {cell_area_m2:.0f} m2")
```

Hold on to that cell area. Every cell count that comes out of `r.watershed`,
accumulation values and the `threshold` you supply alike, converts to ground area
by multiplying by it, and by nothing else.

## Two kinds of hole, handled in opposite ways

This is the single most common mistake in terrain hydrology, and it is a mistake
of conflation rather than of technique. A DEM can have two very different kinds of
problem area, and the correct treatment of one is the wrong treatment of the other.

### NULL gaps must be filled

A NULL cell is missing data: a void in a lidar-derived surface, a hole left by a
cloud mask, a region clipped away by a data provider. `r.watershed` treats NULL
cells as if they were outside the region. Water flows into a gap and never comes
out, so a gap inside your area of interest truncates every flow path that reaches
it and drags the accumulation values downstream to nonsense.

The manual is direct about this: gaps in the elevation map located within the area
of interest must be filled beforehand, for example with `r.fillnulls`.

Punch a 250 m hole in a copy of the DEM, on the main channel, and read the
accumulation at a point downstream of it. The reading point is a cell on the trunk
stream near the southern edge of the region; the section on outlets below shows
how it was found.

```{python}
# | label: null-gap
# The cell carrying the most water in the region: the outlet of the largest
# basin. Both coordinates were derived from the accumulation surface itself
# rather than picked by eye, and the hole sits inside this outlet's own basin,
# 15 km upstream, so the void is genuinely on the path to the checkpoint.
CHECKPOINT = (461595.0, 3900015.0)
HOLE = (446505.0, 3896535.0)


def accumulation_at(raster, coordinates):
    """Read one accumulation value, in cells, at a coordinate pair."""
    result = tools.r_what(map=raster, coordinates=coordinates, format="json")
    return float(result[0][raster]["value"])


# The reference run: the elevation map exactly as it ships.
tools.r_watershed(
    elevation="elevation@PERMANENT",
    threshold=10000,
    accumulation="accum_clean",
    overwrite=True,
)

# The same map with a circular void punched into the channel.
tools.r_mapcalc(
    expression=(
        f"elev_gap = if("
        f"  sqrt((x() - {HOLE[0]})^2 + (y() - {HOLE[1]})^2) < 500,"
        f"  null(),"
        f"  elevation@PERMANENT)"
    ),
    overwrite=True,
)
tools.r_watershed(
    elevation="elev_gap",
    threshold=10000,
    accumulation="accum_gap",
    overwrite=True,
)

voids = int(tools.r_univar(map="elev_gap", format="json")["null_cells"])
print(f"NULL cells punched into the DEM: {voids:,} "
      f"({100 * voids / n_cells:.3f}% of the region)")
print(f"accumulation downstream, clean DEM:  {accumulation_at('accum_clean', CHECKPOINT):>12,.0f}")
print(f"accumulation downstream, gapped DEM: {accumulation_at('accum_gap', CHECKPOINT):>12,.0f}")
```

Two thousand missing cells, a tenth of a percent of the region, and the
contributing area three and a half kilometres downstream is no longer a third of
a million cells. It is negative, which is the module's way of saying the number is
an undercount of unknown size. Water flowed into the void and never came out.

Repair the surface with `r.fillnulls` and rerun. `r.fillnulls` interpolates across
the void with a spline fitted to the surrounding cells. That is an estimate and
should be treated as one, but an estimated surface routes water and a void does
not.

```{python}
# | label: fillnulls
tools.r_fillnulls(
    input="elev_gap",
    output="elev_filled",
    method="bilinear",
    overwrite=True,
)
tools.r_watershed(
    elevation="elev_filled",
    threshold=10000,
    accumulation="accum_filled",
    overwrite=True,
)

filled = int(tools.r_univar(map="elev_filled", format="json")["null_cells"])
print(f"NULL cells after r.fillnulls: {filled:,}")
print(f"accumulation downstream, repaired DEM: {accumulation_at('accum_filled', CHECKPOINT):,.0f}")
```

The downstream value is back where it started. That is the whole argument for
filling gaps: not that the interpolated elevations are right, but that a routed
surface with an estimate in it is worth more than a routed surface with a hole in
it.

### Depressions must not be filled

A depression is different. It is a closed low point in the surface: sometimes a
real one, a sinkhole, a playa, a quarry, a stormwater basin, and very often an
artifact of measurement noise on ground whose true relief is smaller than the
vertical error of the sensor.

The reflex imported from other software is to fill depressions before routing:
raise every pit until water spills over its lowest rim, repeat until nothing is
trapped. Two things happen when you do that. You have edited your measurements to
satisfy an assumption of the algorithm, and you have manufactured flat areas,
sometimes very large ones across a floodplain. Flat means no steepest descent, so
the software falls back on a tie-breaking rule, and the suspiciously straight
parallel channels you have seen in filled-DEM output are that rule showing
through.

`r.watershed` does not need any of it. It uses an A^T least-cost search after
Ehlschlaeger (1989): cells are processed in elevation order, so by the time the
algorithm reaches a cell it already knows the cheapest route out of everything
below it, and it routes flow through the depression by cost rather than filling
it. The manual states the consequence in one sentence: the elevation map need not
be sink-filled because the module uses a least-cost algorithm.

::: {.callout-important}
## Fill the gaps, not the sinks

`r.fillnulls` for NULL gaps: yes, always, before routing.

Sink filling, including `r.fill.dir`, before `r.watershed`: no. It destroys real
topography, invents flat surfaces, and buys you nothing the least-cost search does
not already handle. `r.fill.dir` exists for workflows built around tools that do
require a depressionless surface, which `r.watershed` is not.
:::

The routing does have a limit worth stating plainly. It removes the artifacts that
filling introduces, but it cannot tell a real closed depression from a measurement
error, and it routes through both. If genuine depressions matter to your problem,
supply them explicitly with the `depression=` option, where every non-NULL,
non-zero cell is treated as a real depression that water enters and does not
leave. Nothing in the module will find them for you.

Clean up the demonstration maps so the rest of the guide runs on the real surface.

```{python}
# | label: cleanup-gap
tools.g_remove(
    type="raster",
    name="elev_gap,accum_gap,elev_filled,accum_filled,accum_clean",
    flags="f",
)
```

## The main run

With the region set and the surface understood, the analysis itself is one call.

```{python}
# | label: watershed-run
import time

THRESHOLD = 10000

start = time.perf_counter()
tools.r_watershed(
    elevation="elevation@PERMANENT",
    threshold=THRESHOLD,
    accumulation="accum",
    drainage="drainage",
    stream="streams",
    basin="basins",
    convergence=5,
    overwrite=True,
)
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start

print(f"threshold: {THRESHOLD:,} cells "
      f"= {THRESHOLD * cell_area_m2 / 1e6:.2f} km2 at this resolution")
print(f"runtime:   {elapsed:.1f} s for {n_cells:,} cells")
```

Four rasters come back and they are all views of the same routing:

- `drainage`, the direction each cell sends its water, numbered 1 to 8
  counter-clockwise from north-east,
- `accum`, the number of cells draining through each cell,
- `streams`, the cells whose accumulation crossed the threshold,
- `basins`, the set of cells sharing an exit.

Basins and streams are numbered consistently, so basin 42 drains through stream
segment 42 and you can join the two without a spatial operation.

### Vectorize the network before you map it

The `streams` output is a raster, and a raster stream drawn at 30 m is a
staircase of square cells. Thin it to one cell wide with `r.thin`, then convert
with `r.to.vect`, and you get a real line: it draws cleanly at any scale, it
carries the basin identifier as its category, and it is the form every other
tool expects. Doing this immediately after the run rather than at the end is
also just the honest workflow, because every map below wants the vector.

`r.to.vect -v` preserves the raster value as the vector category, which is what
makes streams and basins joinable without a spatial operation.

```{python}
# | label: vectorize
tools.r_thin(input="streams", output="streams_thin", overwrite=True)
tools.r_to_vect(
    input="streams_thin", output="streams_vect", type="line", flags="v", overwrite=True
)
tools.r_to_vect(
    input="basins", output="basins_vect", type="area", flags="s", overwrite=True
)

print(tools.v_info(map="streams_vect", flags="t").text.strip())
print()
print(tools.v_info(map="basins_vect", flags="t").text.strip())
```

```{python}
# | label: map-overview
tools.r_relief(input="elevation@PERMANENT", output="relief", zscale=2, overwrite=True)

# Basin divides as lines, not fills. Basin ids are nominal categories: a
# sequential colour ramp over them implies that basin 900 is somehow more than
# basin 30, and a random one turns the map into confetti. The divide is the
# information; the terrain underneath is what the reader needs to see.
overview = gj.Map(width=760, use_region=True)
overview.d_rast(map="relief")
overview.d_vect(map="basins_vect", fill_color="none", color="110:110:110", width=1)
overview.d_vect(map="streams_vect", color="40:110:190", width=2)
overview.d_barscale(at=(4, 6))
overview.show()
```

```{python}
# | label: cover
# | echo: false
# | output: false
# Listing thumbnail for this page.
Path("images").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
cover = gj.Map(width=520, filename="images/cover.png", use_region=True)
cover.d_rast(map="relief")
cover.d_vect(map="basins_vect", fill_color="none", color="110:110:110", width=1)
cover.d_vect(map="streams_vect", color="40:110:190", width=2)
```

### Multiple flow direction is the default

`r.watershed` distributes each cell's flow among all its downslope neighbours,
weighted by slope, and includes the least-cost path in that distribution. That is
multiple flow direction, MFD, and it is on by default. The `convergence`
parameter, 1 to 10, controls how tightly the split pulls back together: lower
values spread flow across hillslopes, higher values drive it toward a single path.
The module's default and its documented recommendation are both 5, after Holmgren
(1994).

Single flow direction, the familiar D8, is available with the `-s` flag.

```{python}
# | label: sfd
tools.r_watershed(
    elevation="elevation@PERMANENT",
    threshold=THRESHOLD,
    accumulation="accum_sfd",
    stream="streams_sfd",
    flags="s",
    overwrite=True,
)

mfd_stats = tools.r_univar(map="accum", format="json")
sfd_stats = tools.r_univar(map="accum_sfd", format="json")

print(f"{'':22s}{'MFD':>16s}{'SFD (-s)':>16s}")
for label, key in [("max accumulation", "max"), ("mean of |accumulation|", "mean_of_abs")]:
    print(f"{label:22s}{mfd_stats[key]:>16,.0f}{sfd_stats[key]:>16,.0f}")
```

Which one you want depends on what the output feeds. Single flow gives clean,
one-cell-wide channels, which is what you need if the network is going to be
thinned and vectorized. Multiple flow gives more defensible upslope area on
divergent terrain, alluvial fans and broad convex hillslopes, and is what you want
when accumulation is an input to a wetness, erosion, or stream power index. The
`tci` and `spi` outputs of `r.watershed` are computed from that same routing.

## Read the accumulation raster correctly

Here is the detail that most tutorials skip and most downstream analyses get
wrong. The accumulation raster is signed.

```{python}
# | label: accum-sign
stats = tools.r_univar(map="accum", format="json")
print(f"min:  {stats['min']:>14,.0f}")
print(f"max:  {stats['max']:>14,.0f}")
print(f"mean of absolute values: {stats['mean_of_abs']:,.1f}")

tools.r_mapcalc(expression="underestimated = if(accum < 0, 1, null())", overwrite=True)
neg = tools.r_univar(map="underestimated", format="json")
share = int(neg["n"]) / n_cells * 100
print(f"\ncells with negative accumulation: {int(neg['n']):,} ({share:.1f}% of the region)")
```

A negative value means the cell may receive flow from outside the current
computational region. The magnitude is what the module could see. The sign is the
module telling you the total is a floor, not a measurement.

This has three practical consequences.

**Take the absolute value before you scale or symbolize.** A colour ramp stretched
over the raw range is dominated by the largest negative values and shows you
almost nothing about the positive ones. Use `abs()` in `r.mapcalc`, or the `-a`
flag on `r.watershed`, which forces positive accumulation even for likely
underestimates. Both are fine for display. Neither makes the underlying number
correct.

**Scale the colour table logarithmically, or the map is useless.** This is a
display problem rather than a hydrology one, but it defeats more accumulation
maps than anything else. The distribution is extremely heavy tailed: the median
cell in this region has single digits of contributing area while the trunk
carries hundreds of thousands, six orders of magnitude apart. A linear ramp
spends its entire range on a handful of channel cells and paints everything else
the bottom colour, so the map shows two or three bright threads on a flat field
and hides the network that is the actual result.

`r.colors` has this built in and it is worth knowing rather than rebuilding.
The `-a` flag applies logarithmic-absolute scaling, which handles the absolute
value and the logarithm in one step and works directly on the signed raster, so
there is no intermediate map to create. Adding `-e` equalizes against the
histogram, putting the colour breaks where the cells actually are instead of at
even intervals. Reaching for `r.mapcalc` to build a `log(abs(accum) + 1.0)`
raster works, but it is three commands and two throwaway maps to reproduce two
flags.

Note what `-a` does not do. It changes how the raster is drawn and nothing else.
The values underneath are still signed, and a negative one still means the
number is a floor rather than a measurement.

**And show it at a scale that can hold it.** The map below is a detail window,
not the whole region, and that is deliberate. Accumulation is a texture rather
than a set of shapes: the whole 62 by 73 km area rendered to the width of this
page works out at roughly 80 m per pixel, so the first-order drainage is finer
than a single pixel and turns into speckle. Basin and stream maps survive the
regional view because they are structural. This one does not, and no colour
ramp rescues a map asked to draw detail below its own resolution.

**Do not read negative magnitudes as contributing area.** They are undercounts of
an unknown amount. Turning them positive to make a map render and then quoting the
value as a drainage area is the most common way to get a confidently wrong number
out of this tool.

**Use the sign as a diagnostic.** The manual suggests exactly this: intersect the
negative cells with the basin map to see which basins are compromised.

```{python}
# | label: problem-basins
tools.r_mapcalc(
    expression="problem_basins = if(accum < 0, basins, null())", overwrite=True
)

all_basins = tools.r_info(map="basins", format="json")
affected = tools.r_stats(input="problem_basins", flags="n").text
affected_ids = {line.split()[0] for line in affected.strip().splitlines() if line.strip()}

print(f"basin values present: 2 to {int(all_basins['max'])}")
print(f"basins touched by flow from outside the region: {len(affected_ids)}")
```

If those basins are the ones you care about, the fix is not a parameter. Enlarge
the computational region until the whole contributing area is inside it, rerun,
and clip afterwards. For a headwater catchment the analysis extent and the area of
interest are the same box. For anything on a mainstem they are not, and the buffer
you need can be far larger than the site.

```{python}
# | label: map-accumulation
# -a is logarithmic-absolute scaling: it takes the absolute value and the
# logarithm together, straight onto the raw accumulation raster, so there is no
# intermediate map to build, name or clean up.
#
# Not -e. Histogram equalization spreads the CELLS evenly across the ramp, so
# half the map lands in the dark half. That is right for imagery and wrong
# here: most cells are hillslope and should stay pale, with the ramp saved for
# the channels.
tools.r_colors(map="accum", color="blues", flags="a")

# A detail window around the San Francisco Peaks. At the full 62 by 73 km the
# drainage texture is finer than one screen pixel and renders as noise, which
# is a property of the display scale rather than of the data.
tools.g_region(n=3910000, s=3888000, w=433000, e=458000, align="elevation@PERMANENT")

acc_map = gj.Map(width=760, use_region=True)
acc_map.d_shade(shade="relief", color="accum", brighten=-10)
acc_map.d_barscale(at=(4, 6))
acc_map.show()

# Back to the whole region for everything that follows.
tools.g_region(raster="elevation@PERMANENT")
```

## The threshold is a decision, not a discovery

Nothing in an elevation raster says where a stream begins. `threshold` is you
saying it: the minimum size of an exterior basin, counted in cells when no `flow`
map is supplied, and with it the level of detail in the stream network.

Run the same DEM at two thresholds and measure the difference.

```{python}
# | label: threshold-sweep
import math

def network_summary(threshold, suffix):
    """Run r.watershed at one threshold and summarize the network it produces."""
    tools.r_watershed(
        elevation="elevation@PERMANENT",
        threshold=threshold,
        stream=f"streams_{suffix}",
        basin=f"basins_{suffix}",
        overwrite=True,
    )
    stream_cells = int(tools.r_univar(map=f"streams_{suffix}", format="json")["n"])
    basin_max = int(tools.r_info(map=f"basins_{suffix}", format="json")["max"])
    # r.watershed labels basins with even integers, so the count is half the maximum.
    basin_count = basin_max // 2
    area_km2 = n_cells * cell_area_m2 / 1e6
    # Approximate channel length: cell count times cell size, ignoring diagonal steps.
    length_km = stream_cells * region["nsres"] / 1000
    return {
        "threshold": threshold,
        "min basin km2": threshold * cell_area_m2 / 1e6,
        "basins": basin_count,
        "stream cells": stream_cells,
        "drainage density km/km2": length_km / area_km2,
    }

rows = [network_summary(10000, "10k"), network_summary(500, "500")]

header = list(rows[0])
print("".join(f"{h:>24s}" for h in header))
for row in rows:
    print("".join(
        f"{row[h]:>24,.2f}" if isinstance(row[h], float) else f"{row[h]:>24,}"
        for h in header
    ))
```

Both runs completed without error, took about the same time, and produced maps
that look equally authoritative. The basin count differs by a factor of nearly
twenty and the drainage density by more than four, and so does every per-basin
statistic you would compute afterward. Neither run is wrong. They answer different
questions, and only you know which question you asked.

```{python}
# | label: map-threshold
# What differs between the two runs is drainage density, so draw the networks
# rather than the basins. Both vectorized the same way, so the comparison is
# between the two thresholds and not between two rendering styles.
for suffix in ("10k", "500"):
    tools.r_thin(input=f"streams_{suffix}", output=f"thin_{suffix}", overwrite=True)
    tools.r_to_vect(
        input=f"thin_{suffix}",
        output=f"vect_{suffix}",
        type="line",
        flags="v",
        overwrite=True,
    )

coarse = gj.Map(width=400, use_region=True)
coarse.d_rast(map="relief")
coarse.d_vect(map="vect_10k", color="40:110:190", width=2)
coarse.d_text(text="threshold = 10000", at=(4, 94), size=5, color="black")
coarse.show()

fine = gj.Map(width=400, use_region=True)
fine.d_rast(map="relief")
fine.d_vect(map="vect_500", color="40:110:190", width=2)
fine.d_text(text="threshold = 500", at=(4, 94), size=5, color="black")
fine.show()
```

There is no correct threshold in general. There are defensible ones for a purpose:
matched to the drainage density of a mapped reference network in the same
physiographic region, matched to field-verified channel heads, or matched to
whatever the downstream analysis assumes about basin size. If the number came from
a tutorial, including this one, say so in your methods.

::: {.callout-tip}
## The first question about any terrain-derived stream network

It is not whether the network is accurate. It is what threshold produced it. Two
networks over the same DEM can look nothing alike and both be correct.
:::

### Exterior and interior basins are not the same thing

`threshold` sets the minimum size of an *exterior* basin: a basin whose stream has
at least that many cells flowing into it, which in practice means a headwater
basin. Interior basins are the strips between two junctions, and their size is set
by how far apart those junctions happen to fall, which you did not choose. Expect
a basin map with tidy headwater polygons and a few long awkward ones lower down,
and do not read anything into the contrast.

The `half_basin` output splits each basin along its stream into left-bank and
right-bank halves, with right-hand cells taking even values matching `basin` and
left-hand cells taking the odd value one below. It is more useful than it sounds
when aspect matters, because the two banks of a creek can face opposite directions
and behave like different hillslopes.

## Resolution changes the science, silently

`threshold` is counted in cells. The region resolution converts cells to ground
area. Change the resolution and keep the threshold and you have changed the model
without touching the parameter you thought controlled it.

```{python}
# | label: resolution
def run_at_resolution(res, suffix):
    tools.g_region(raster="elevation@PERMANENT", res=res, flags="a")
    reg = tools.g_region(flags="p", format="json")
    cells = reg["rows"] * reg["cols"]
    tools.r_watershed(
        elevation="elevation@PERMANENT",
        threshold=10000,
        stream=f"streams_res{suffix}",
        basin=f"basins_res{suffix}",
        overwrite=True,
    )
    basin_max = int(tools.r_info(map=f"basins_res{suffix}", format="json")["max"])
    stream_cells = int(
        tools.r_univar(map=f"streams_res{suffix}", format="json")["n"]
    )
    return {
        "resolution m": int(reg["nsres"]),
        "cells in region": cells,
        "10000 cells = km2": 10000 * reg["nsres"] * reg["ewres"] / 1e6,
        "basins": basin_max // 2,
        "stream cells": stream_cells,
    }


# 30 m is the native resolution of this DEM. Going finer would interpolate
# detail the data does not contain, so the comparison is native against coarser.
res_rows = [run_at_resolution(30, "30"), run_at_resolution(90, "90")]

# Put the region back where it was.
tools.g_region(raster="elevation@PERMANENT")

header = list(res_rows[0])
print("".join(f"{h:>22s}" for h in header))
for row in res_rows:
    print("".join(
        f"{row[h]:>22,.2f}" if isinstance(row[h], float) else f"{row[h]:>22,}"
        for h in header
    ))
```

Same DEM, same `threshold=10000`, two different minimum basin sizes and two
different networks. Nothing in the call changed. This is the strongest argument
for writing the region settings into your methods section next to the parameters,
and for setting the region explicitly at the top of every script rather than
inheriting whatever the last command left behind.

Resolution also decides what can exist at all. At 30 m a 4 m incised swale is not
rendered coarsely, it is absent, and so is the flow path through it. At 1 m you
resolve the channel, and also the curb, the berm, the parked vehicle, and the
bridge deck, which is not unambiguously good news: fine lidar produces far more
spurious depressions, far more compute, and it turns structures water passes under
into barriers the model cannot pass. Channel length in particular is a function of
cell size and is not comparable across grids.

Note which direction this comparison runs. 30 m is what this DEM actually
contains, so the coarser run is the honest half of the pair: resampling to 90 m
throws detail away, which is a thing you might really do for a regional run.
Resampling the other way, to 10 m, would invent detail the source never had, and
the resulting network would look finer while meaning less.

### One basin above one point

When you need the catchment draining to a specific location rather than the whole
tessellation, `r.water.outlet` walks the drainage raster upstream from a
coordinate. The outlet must sit on a stream cell, so pick it from the network you
just computed rather than from a map click.

```{python}
# | label: outlet
# Find the cell with the largest fully-contained contributing area.
tools.r_mapcalc(
    expression="accum_pos = if(accum > 0, accum, null())", overwrite=True
)
cells = tools.r_stats(input="accum_pos", flags="gn").text
east, north, value = max(
    (line.split() for line in cells.strip().splitlines()),
    key=lambda parts: float(parts[2]),
)

print(f"outlet: {east} E, {north} N")
print(f"contributing area: {float(value):,.0f} cells "
      f"= {float(value) * cell_area_m2 / 1e6:.1f} km2")

tools.r_water_outlet(
    input="drainage",
    output="outlet_basin",
    coordinates=(east, north),
    overwrite=True,
)

basin_cells = int(tools.r_univar(map="outlet_basin", format="json")["n"])
disagreement = abs(basin_cells - float(value)) / float(value) * 100
print(f"r.water.outlet basin: {basin_cells:,} cells "
      f"= {basin_cells * cell_area_m2 / 1e6:.1f} km2")
print(f"disagreement with the accumulation value: {disagreement:.2f}%")
```

The two areas are close but not identical, and the reason is instructive.
`r.water.outlet` walks the single-direction `drainage` raster upstream and counts
whole cells, while the accumulation value at that cell is the MFD total, which
includes fractional contributions split across neighbours. Exact agreement is not
expected. A disagreement of a fraction of a percent, as here, says the outlet sits
on the channel. A disagreement of tens of percent says it does not, and the
usual cause is an outlet coordinate picked from a basemap rather than from the
computed stream network.

```{python}
# | label: map-outlet
# One region is the subject here, so a fill is the right call. A single warm
# tone against the grey terrain, rather than a ramp over a map with one value.
basin_rules = Path("outlet.rules")
basin_rules.write_text("0% 208:121:68\n100% 208:121:68\n")
tools.r_colors(map="outlet_basin", rules=str(basin_rules))
basin_rules.unlink()

outlet_map = gj.Map(width=760, use_region=True)
outlet_map.d_rast(map="relief")
outlet_map.d_shade(shade="relief", color="outlet_basin", brighten=0)
outlet_map.d_vect(map="streams_vect", color="40:110:190", width=2)
outlet_map.d_barscale(at=(4, 6))
outlet_map.show()
```

## Scaling up

`r.watershed` ships as two implementations of the same algorithm. The default runs
in memory and is fast. The `-m` flag switches to the segmented, disk-swapping
version, which uses only as much RAM as `memory=` allows and pages the rest
through disk files.

That flag is the reason this module handles DEMs that do not fit in RAM. The
in-memory version tops out at about 2 billion cells; the segmented version at
9.2 billion billion. The trade is speed, and the manual is blunt that the
segmented mode is slow.

```{python}
# | label: disk-swap
start = time.perf_counter()
tools.r_watershed(
    elevation="elevation@PERMANENT",
    threshold=THRESHOLD,
    accumulation="accum_seg",
    memory=500,
    flags="m",
    overwrite=True,
)
seg_elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start

print(f"in-memory: {elapsed:.1f} s")
print(f"disk swap: {seg_elapsed:.1f} s (memory=500 MB)")
```

On five million cells the swap version is pure overhead. On a national DEM it is
the difference between a result and an out-of-memory error. Two other levers help
before you reach for it: mask out the area you do not need, since NULL cells are
skipped entirely, and consider running at a coarser resolution built from
`r.resamp.stats` minimum values rather than a plain resample, so the coarse cells
still carry the valley floors.

## Bring your own data

The workflow does not change when the DEM does. What changes is that you now own
the vertical accuracy, the surface definition, and the extent, which is where the
real failure modes live.

The cell below is not executed as part of this page, because it downloads from an
external service that would make the page's build depend on a third party. Run it
yourself against any GeoTIFF you have.

```{python}
# | label: byo-data
# | eval: false
# Import a DEM tile into a new project, then run the same analysis.
# 1) Create a project whose CRS is read from the tile itself.
project = Path.home() / "grassdata" / "my_watershed"
gs.create_project(project, filename="dem.tif")

# 2) Start a session and import, reprojecting if needed.
session = gj.init(project / "PERMANENT")
tools.r_import(input="dem.tif", output="dem", resample="bilinear")

# 3) Set the region from the imported map. This fixes the model grid.
tools.g_region(raster="dem")

# 4) Fill NULL gaps, and only NULL gaps.
tools.r_fillnulls(input="dem", output="dem_nogaps", method="bilinear")

# 5) Route. Choose the threshold from the cell size, not from this page.
tools.r_watershed(
    elevation="dem_nogaps",
    threshold=10000,
    accumulation="accum",
    drainage="drainage",
    stream="streams",
    basin="basins",
)
```

Three checks before you trust the output of that run.

**Was the DEM ground-classified?** A bare-earth model and a first-return surface
model look similar in a hillshade and behave nothing alike here. On a surface
model a wooded riparian corridor is a ridge, so the computed channel climbs out of
the valley and runs down the hillside beside it. USGS 3DEP is bare earth. Many
photogrammetric and radar products are not.

**Is the extent bigger than the question?** Check the negative accumulation cells
first, before anything else. If they reach into the basins you care about, the
analysis extent is too small and no parameter will fix it.

**Is the terrain steep enough to have an opinion?** Direction comes from the
elevation difference between adjacent cells. A coastal-plain floodplain at a 0.02
percent gradient falls about 2 mm across a 10 m cell, while the published vertical
accuracy of national 10 m elevation data is on the order of a metre. The noise is
two orders of magnitude larger than the fall, and whatever direction those cells
receive did not come from the terrain. The symptoms are recognizable: channels
that wander or braid across a floodplain, or basin boundaries that move hundreds
of metres when you change nothing but the elevation source. What fixes it is
different data, not a different flag.

## Honest limits

The rasters look more authoritative than they are. This section is the one to read
twice.

**There is no water in any of it.** No rainfall, no infiltration, no soil, no
evaporation, no time. An accumulation of 20,000 is 20,000 upslope cells. It is not
litres per second, it does not become litres per second without a rainfall-runoff
model on top of it, and the size of the number does not make it a discharge. The
`flow=` option lets you weight the accumulation by a per-cell quantity, a runoff
coefficient or an effective rainfall depth, and that is as close as this module
gets. It is not close: there is still no time axis, no routing velocity, and no
storage.

**It knows nothing about what was buried or built.** A DEM contains the road
embankment and not the culvert under it, the bridge deck and not the opening
beneath it, the parking lot and not the storm drain, the field and not the tile.
Flow piles up against the embankment and exits somewhere no water goes. In urban
and agricultural settings this is the single largest source of wrong answers, and
nothing in the output flags it.

**It is not a floodplain map.** No depth, no extent, no velocity, no return
period, no hydraulics of any kind. A delineated basin tells you what area drains
to a point. It says nothing about what happens when it rains on that area.

**It carries no regulatory standing.** A terrain-derived boundary will not match
the published hydrography, the National Hydrography Dataset and Watershed Boundary
Dataset in the United States or your national equivalent, unless you deliberately
make it match. A reviewer who expects the published delineation will not accept a
different one because the terrain says so.

**It cannot tell you it was wrong.** The module produces a complete,
plausible-looking result from a bad DEM with exactly the confidence it produces
one from a good DEM. There is no internal check on the input. The negative
accumulation convention is the only warning it issues about anything.

**Water that moves against the terrain is invisible.** Interbasin transfers,
canals, pumped systems, reservoir releases, and diversions all move water across
divides the surface says are closed.

### Where r.watershed is the wrong tool

Reaching for a different tool is not a failure of this one. The cases are specific.

| If you need | Use instead |
|-------------|-------------|
| A stream network with explicit topology, node and link identifiers, and Strahler or Horton ordering | [`r.stream.extract`](https://grass.osgeo.org/grass-stable/manuals/r.stream.extract.html) and the `r.stream.*` addon suite. `r.watershed` gives you segments numbered to match basins, not an ordered network. |
| Overland flow with a time axis, depth, or a rainfall event | [`r.sim.water`](https://grass.osgeo.org/grass-stable/manuals/r.sim.water.html), a path-sampling shallow-water solver, or a hydrodynamic model outside GRASS. Accumulation is not a hydrograph. |
| Flow paths through culverts, storm drains, or tile | A hydraulic or pipe-network model, or a DEM you have burned the structures into by hand. No terrain-only method can recover them. |
| A wetness index from a filled, depressionless surface because a downstream model requires one | [`r.fill.dir`](https://grass.osgeo.org/grass-stable/manuals/r.fill.dir.html), knowing exactly what it costs you, or [`r.topidx`](https://grass.osgeo.org/grass-stable/manuals/r.topidx.html) if the topographic index is the actual goal. |
| A basin boundary that matches a published one | The published dataset. Terrain analysis is how you understand the boundary, not how you replace it. |
| Massive DEMs where throughput matters more than accuracy on low slopes | [`r.terraflow`](https://grass.osgeo.org/grass-stable/manuals/r.terraflow.html), with the caveat from the `r.watershed` manual that it performs worse on flat terrain and on canopy-contaminated surfaces. |

## Reproducing this page

The whole guide runs from a package-manager install of GRASS and one public
dataset. Nothing above is cached from an earlier state: the outputs shown were
produced by executing this document, against the software versions printed at the
top.

To repeat it end to end, install GRASS, run the cells in order, and expect the
numbers to match exactly. `r.watershed` is deterministic: the same DEM, region,
and parameters give the same rasters every time. That is a low bar, and a great
deal of published terrain analysis does not clear it, usually because the region
settings were never written down.

```{python}
# | label: cleanup
tools.g_remove(
    type="raster",
    name=(
        "streams_res30,basins_res30,streams_res90,basins_res90,"
        "accum_pos,accum_seg,thin_10k,thin_500,"
        "underestimated,problem_basins"
    ),
    flags="f",
)
```

1989. <http://chuck.ehlschlaeger.info/older/IGIS/paper.html>

grid based elevation models: an empirical evaluation. *Hydrological Processes*,

stream network analysis for the Chagres River basin, Republic of Panama. In R.
Harmon (Ed.), *The Rio Chagres: A Multidisciplinary Profile of a Tropical
Watershed* (pp. 83-95). Springer.

Metz, M., Mitasova, H., & Harmon, R. S. (2011). Efficient extraction of drainage

<https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-15-667-2011>

Quinn, P., Beven, K., Chevallier, P., & Planchon, O. (1991). The prediction of
hillslope flow paths for distributed hydrological modelling using digital
elevation models. *Hydrological Processes*, 5(1), 59-79.
<https://doi.org/10.1002/hyp.3360050106>

GRASS Development Team. (2026). *Geographic Resources Analysis Support System
(GRASS) Software*. Open Source Geospatial Foundation.
<https://grass.osgeo.org>

Cite the method as well as the software. `r.watershed` is Ehlschlaeger's A^T
least-cost search with Metz's sorting and MFD implementation, and a methods
section that names only "GRASS" has left out the part a reader needs in order to
reproduce or to disagree with you.
